studies.Reference: Dietary Intake of Branched Chain Amino Acids and Breast Cancer Risk in the NHS and NHS II Prospective Cohorts.
studies.Authors: Tobias DK, Chai B, Tamimi RM, Manson JE, Hu FB, Willett WC, Eliassen AH
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Average intakes of total and individual BCAAs ... were estimated from repeated diet questionnaires

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Our analyses included 196 161 women from the Nurses' Health Study and Nurses' Health Study II longitudinal cohorts.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: the hazard ratio of breast cancer for those in the top quintile was 1.05 (95% confidence interval = 0.98 to 1.12; 2-sided P trend = .20)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: No associations between dietary intakes of total or individual BCAAs with breast cancer risk were observed.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: incident self-reported breast cancer cases were confirmed via medical record review
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Average intakes of total and individual BCAAs (isoleucine, leucine, valine) were estimated from repeated diet questionnaires

studies.Reference: Circulating branched-chain amino acids and long-term risk of obesity-related cancers in women.
studies.Authors: Tobias DK, Hazra A, Lawler PR, Chandler PD, Chasman DI, Buring JE, Lee IM, Cheng S, Manson JE, Mora S
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: BCAAs were quantified via NMR spectroscopy, log-transformed, and standardized.

extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: modest association for leucine with obesity-related cancers (1.04 [1.00-1.08])
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: positive associations between leucine and postmenopausal breast cancer
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=0.046.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: positive associations between leucine and postmenopausal breast cancer
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: BCAAs were quantified via NMR spectroscopy, log-transformed, and standardized.

studies.Reference: Dietary intake of branched-chain amino acids in relation to the risk of breast cancer.
studies.Authors: Nouri-Majd S, Salari-Moghaddam A, Benisi-Kohansal S, Azadbakht L, Esmaillzadeh A
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: We assessed dietary intakes using the validated 106-item Willett-format semi-quantitative dish-based food frequency questionnaire.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Overall 1050 women including 350 patients and 700 controls were included.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: women in the highest quartile of BCAAs had lower odds of breast cancer compared with the first quartile (OR: 0.50; 95% CI 0.34-0.72)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: women in the highest quartile of BCAAs had lower odds of breast cancer
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=2.930e-04.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: Breast cancer was diagnosed by physical examination, mammography and pathological confirmation.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: The total intake of valine, leucine, and isoleucine from all food items in the questionnaire was used to calculate BCAAs intake.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Insufficient studies to perform formal publication bias testing.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 0.77 (95% CI: 0.4–1.48), indicating no statistically significant association between BCAAs and breast cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 92.75%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
